n: Ahaz becomes king of Judah about 735 BC (counting from a co-regency with Jotham). He is the king to whom Isaiah gave the famous Immanuel sign.

f.g: ‘he has grasped’; a shortened form of Jehoahaz.

n: He took the throne at twenty and reigned sixteen years. Unlike his father and grandfather, he did not do what was right.
Ahaz imitated Israel’s idolatry and even sacrificed his own son in fire, a Canaanite practice the law strictly forbade. This was a new low for David’s line.

f.w: made his son to pass through the fire
f.g: sacrificed his son by fire, likely to Molech.

n: He worshiped at hilltop shrines and pagan sacred groves throughout the land.
Rezin of Aram and Pekah of Israel besiege Jerusalem, trying to force Judah into their anti-Assyrian alliance. They fail to take the city, as Isaiah promised Ahaz they would.
Aram drives Judah out of Elath, the Red Sea port, and Edomites settle there. (Many manuscripts read “Edom” for “Syria”—the Hebrew words look almost identical.)

f.g: Hebrew Aram; likely a scribal slip for Edom, which looks similar in Hebrew.

n: Instead of trusting the Lord as Isaiah urged, Ahaz appeals to Tiglath-pileser: “I am your servant and your son.” He voluntarily makes Judah an Assyrian vassal.

f.w: I am thy servant and thy son
f.g: the language of a vassal submitting to an overlord.

n: He empties the temple and palace treasuries to pay Assyria.
Assyria crushes Damascus (732 BC), deports its people to Kir, and kills Rezin. The Aramean kingdom that had troubled Israel for two centuries comes to an end, as Amos had foretold.

f.g: a region in Mesopotamia, the Arameans’ original homeland.

n: Ahaz goes to Damascus to pay homage to the Assyrian king. Admiring an altar he sees there, he sends its design to Urijah the priest.
Urijah builds a copy before the king returns. The high priest goes along without objection.
Ahaz returns and personally offers sacrifices on the new altar.
He offers all the main types of sacrifice on it. The forms of worship remain, but the pattern is now borrowed from a pagan capital.

f.g: fellowship offerings shared in a meal.

n: He moves Solomon’s bronze altar, the one built according to God’s pattern, out of its central place and off to the side.

f.g: the bronze altar of burnt offering made under Solomon.

n: All the daily, royal, and public sacrifices go on the new “great altar.” Ahaz keeps the old bronze altar for his private use “to inquire by”—perhaps for omens, a pagan practice.

f.g: possibly to seek omens by examining sacrifices, an Assyrian practice.

n: Urijah complies with everything.
Ahaz strips the bronze panels from the temple’s wheeled stands and takes the great bronze basin off its twelve bronze oxen—probably to pay more tribute to Assyria.

f.g: the huge bronze water basin in the temple court.

n: He also removes a covered Sabbath structure and the king’s private entrance to the temple, “because of the king of Assyria”—to please his overlord or remove signs of independent kingship.
His other acts are in Judah’s chronicles; 2 Chronicles 28 adds that he shut the temple doors.

f.w: the rest of the acts of Ahaz

n: Ahaz dies, and his son Hezekiah—one of Judah’s greatest kings—succeeds him.
